title: Shadow KV page reclaimer and adaptive compression (draft)
content:
Summary:

This doc proposes an end-to-end design for a lightweight shadow reclaimer that cooperates with OS-level paging and an adaptive compression layer for KV cache entries when we must spill to host memory over PCIe/UMA. Goal is to reduce PCIe bandwidth pressure, bound tail latency caused by host-pagebacks, and dynamically pick placement and prefetching thresholds based on workload characteristics.

Motivation / background:

We currently observe two recurring issues when serving large-context models with KV caches:
1) Spiky PCIe traffic and unpredictable host page-fault stalls when the working set exceeds GPU residency.
2) Wasteful roundtrips when evicted KV pages are accessed shortly after eviction (referred as redeal), which amplifies latency for tail requests.

Existing notes focus on hysteresis and static thresholds. This draft explores a different angle: rather than purely threshold-based host evictions, run a background shadow reclaimer that maintains lightweight metadata estimates of recency and frequency and also optionally compresses cold KV slabs before writing to host memory. Combine that with NUMA-aware residency and a small OS-cooperative hint API to reduce page-fault penalties.

Design goals:
- Keep critical-path generation latency within SLOs for 99.9% requests despite spillback.
- Reduce average PCIe bytes transferred per token for spill-heavy workloads by >= 25% vs uncompressed spills.
- Bound CPU memory fragmentation and avoid OS thrashing by organizing host-resident slabs with compact headers.
- Maintain compatibility with Dedicated / Private deployments (no privileged kernel modules).

Terminology:
- KV slab: contiguous allocation of kv entries for a set of layers or batches; unit of eviction.
- Shadow reclaimer: async component that decides candidates for eviction and manages compressed spill layout.
- Cold score: a small 8-bit estimate per slab combining recency and reuse probability.
- Soft-threshold or hard-threshold: soft threshold triggers background reclaimer; hard threshold forces synchronous eviction on allocation failure.

Architecture overview:

Request path -> serving runtime scheduler -> GPU KV cache (resident)

background: shadow reclaimer + compression worker(s) -> host backing store (NUMA-aware)

kernel cooperation: optional madvise-like hint to OS to pre-populate page mappings for hot host slabs (see OS hints section)

Components:
1) Access telemetry and sketching
- Maintain a coarse-grain LRU-ish ring per backend with probabilistic sampling: for every N allocations (N configurable, default 128), sample the slab id and bump its recency counter (8-bit saturating age).
- Also record a small reuse histogram (3 buckets): immediate (<16 tokens), short (16-256 tokens), long (>256 tokens). These are aggregated over sliding windows of 60s.

2) Shadow reclaimer (async)
- Runs on a separate worker pool pinned to CPU cores on the same NUMA node as the GPU if possible.
- Periodically (configurable interval default 250ms) inspects slab scores and attempts to reach a target free-resident ratio.
- For candidate slabs: try to compress them in-memory first. If compressed size is less than compression-benefit-threshold (default 0.75), schedule compressed write to host. Else write raw slab.
- Writing is done with batched DMA-friendly page-aligned buffers to reduce PCIe transaction overheads. We coalesce multiple small slabs into a single contiguous host allocation with a sub-allocation table in header to reduce fragmentation.

3) Adaptive compression layer
- Two modes: fast (LZ4-like, CPU-optimal) and slow (zstd-level2, better ratio). Default: use fast for everything; switch to slow for slabs that have very high cold-score and large size (>1MB).
- Compression metadata is kept in the slab header: compressed_len, uncompressed_len, compression_algo_id, cold_score_snapshot.
- Decompression happens on-demand during pageback; the decompressor runs on CPU worker pinned to a different core pool so not to disturb main scheduler threads.

4) NUMA-aware placement and PCIe shaping
- Host backing store allocations attempt to prefer the NUMA node local to GPU host bridge when honoured by hypervisor or OS. Validate by numa node heuristics.
- For multi-GPU hosts, prefer allocation on node where originating GPU is attached. When not possible, mark slab for longer prefetch timeouts and avoid immediate paging-in attempts.
- PCIe shaping: enforce per-device burst quotas and introduce interleaving so we do not saturate host to GPU PCIe links when recovering multiple slabs concurrently. Configurable token-bucket: burst_bytes 128MiB, refill 64MiB per second per GPU as default.

5) OS hints and cooperative prefetch API
- Expose a lightweight hint API: runtime to host-agent: prefetch(slab_id_list, urgency). Host-agent will madvise MADV_WILLNEED or use userfaultfd to wire pages depending on platform privileges. For Private deployments without host-agent, runtime falls back to asynchronous DMA reads at lower priority.
- Rationale: userfaultfd requires privileges; keep it optional. The API decouples runtime policy from host-level mechanics.

Eviction and fetch path (fast-path interaction):
- Normal allocation path checks resident budget. If under soft threshold, signal reclaimer and proceed; otherwise if allocation would cross hard threshold, synchronously evict candidate slabs chosen by the reclaimer's top-of-queue.
- When a generation path requests a KV slab not resident: schedule decompressor and DMA copy; return a placeholder token to scheduler that yields until ready. We keep a fast failover policy: if fetch latency would exceed per-request tail budget, reply with fallback smaller model variant or synthesized response.

Numeric thresholds and suggested defaults as starting point for experiments:
- resident_target_ratio: 0.82
- soft_threshold: 0.9 * gpu_mem_capacity
- hard_threshold: 0.97 * gpu_mem_capacity
- compression-benefit-threshold: 0.75
- sample_interval: 250ms for reclaimer loop; compaction window: 5s for coalescing writes.
- pci_burst_bytes: 134217728 (128MiB), pci_refill_rate: 67108864 (64MiB per second).

Metrics to collect for rollouts:
- pci_bytes_in out per gpu (1s and 1m histograms)
- compressed_spill_bytes and raw_spill_bytes
- spill_recall_rate (fraction of spilled slabs that are rereferenced within 10s)
- avg_eviction_latency, avg_decompression_latency (P50 P95 P99)
- host_fragmentation_ratio (free_bytes over total_bytes in host pool)

Experiments and evaluation plan:
- Phase A: microbenchmarks. Synthetic traces with controlled re reference distributions to validate compression benefit and spill recall rate. Vary sequence lengths batch sizes and request concurrency.
- Phase B: replay production traces anonymized. Measure tail latency under different resident target ratio and compression presets. Key hypothesis: compressed spills reduce PCIe bytes by at least 25 percent and reduce mean pageback time by at least 20 percent due to lower transfer size.
- Phase C: Canary on Dedicated single region. Observe client SLOs for 72 hours with reclaimer defaults compare against control without compression.

Fallback and safety:
- If decompressor misses (corrupt header) fallback to raw read path. All compressed writes have a checksum in header.
- Provide a config knob to disable compression per customer for low latency customers that prefer no extra CPU work.

Compatibility notes:
- Must work in Private deployments without host-agent; there we use lower priority async reads and avoid userfaultfd.
- No kernel module required. We rely on user space DMA APIs and standard POSIX allocation. For high performance on some clouds use available pre registered memory pools where possible.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- How aggressive should compression be? CPU cost versus PCIe reduction tradeoff depends heavily on slab size and model architecture. We should instrument CPU per token overhead versus saved PCIe transfer time on representative instance types.
- What is the right unit size for coalescing slabs? Larger coalesced writes reduce PCIe overhead but increase host fragmentation.
- Should we integrate reinforcement learning style policy to choose eviction compression strategy per customer? Could be overkill.
- Interaction with platform level swap and cgroup memory limits needs more testing; we must not trigger OOM killer by mistake when coalescing heavy host writes.

Implementation roadmap high level:
- Week 0-2: telemetry shims and sampling counters and simple async reclaimer that writes uncompressed slabs to host.
- Week 3-6: compressed spill pipeline fast mode and slab header format and coalesced write path.
- Week 7-10: NUMA-aware allocator and PCIe burst shaper. Performance testing and synthetic workloads.
- Week 11-14: Optional OS hint API and canary.

Rollout plan:
- Start as an opt in feature flag disabled by default. Enable for experimental clusters with telemetry enabled. After meeting traffic and SLO goals in canary flip to on for selected Dedicated customers.

TODOs:
- Finalize slab header layout fields and byte offsets.
- Add checksum and versioning to avoid decoder mismatch.
- Create microbench harness for replaying slab access traces ENG-1298.
- Add grafana dashboards for spill metrics and PCIe shaping headroom.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic focused on CPU side cooperation rather than kernel level changes. Given the diversity of deployment environments cloud and on prem optional host agent features are helpful but we must ensure correctness without them.
- I'm interested in feedback around compression presets LZ4 versus zstd and whether per layer policies some layers are cheaper to recompute than others should be integrated into the cold score.
